nameStory: The name 'Snaketongue Truffleclub' perfectly captures this fungus's bizarre appearance - it looks like a thin, dark snake's tongue poking up from the ground. The 'truffle' part refers to its parasitic relationship with underground truffle-like fungi, while 'club' describes its simple, club-shaped fruiting body that emerges above ground.
description: Snaketongue Truffleclub is a parasitic fungus that creates slender, dark club-shaped structures poking up from the forest floor. This unusual fungus doesn't feed on dead wood or leaves like many mushrooms - instead, it's a parasite that attacks underground truffle-like fungi called Elaphomyces. The visible part above ground is typically dark brown to black and has a simple, elongated club shape. While not toxic, it's considered inedible and has a tough, leathery texture.

idTips.label: Club-shaped fruiting body
idTips.description: Slender, dark brown to black clubs that emerge from soil, feeling firm and leathery to the touch with a smooth or slightly wrinkled surface

idTips.label: Underground connection
idTips.description: If you carefully dig around the base, you'll often find it attached to a round, warty underground truffle (Elaphomyces) that feels rock-hard

idTips.label: Simple structure
idTips.description: Lacks the cap-and-stem structure of typical mushrooms - just a plain club with no distinct head or branching

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Usually just a few inches tall, easy to overlook among fallen leaves and forest debris

idTips.label: Solitary growth
idTips.description: Typically found alone or in small scattered groups, never forming large clusters like many other fungi

habitat: Look for Snaketongue Truffleclub in mature deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly under oaks, maples, and other hardwoods. It prefers well-drained, slightly acidic soils where its host truffles (Elaphomyces) live underground. You're most likely to spot these dark clubs emerging from leaf litter in established woodlands rather than young or disturbed forests.

seasonality.spring: Early fruiting bodies may begin emerging as soil warms, appearing as small dark bumps pushing through leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season when mature club-shaped bodies are most visible and easiest to identify above ground.
seasonality.fall: Fruiting continues into autumn, though specimens may become weathered and harder to spot among fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions typically die back, though the parasitic relationship continues underground with the host truffle.

funFact: This fungus is essentially a underground vampire - it slowly kills its truffle host from the inside out over several years, then sends up its snake-like fruiting body like a victory flag to announce its successful conquest!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small, dark club fungi like carbon antlers (Xylaria species), but those grow on dead wood while Snaketongue Truffleclub emerges directly from soil. Memory trick: if it's growing on a log or stick, it's not a Snaketongue Truffleclub - this species only grows from dirt where it can reach its underground truffle victims.
contextualKnowledge: This species has had several scientific name changes and is sometimes called 'goldenthread cordyceps' in traditional medicine contexts, though it's completely different from the famous Cordyceps fungi that parasitize insects. The name shuffle reflects ongoing research into fungal relationships and classification.
compareHints: Compared to its relative Drumstick Truffleclub, Snaketongue Truffleclub has a more slender, elongated appearance rather than a swollen drumstick shape. While both species parasitize underground fungi, Snaketongue Truffleclub specifically targets Elaphomyces truffles and tends to be darker in color with a smoother surface texture than its clubbier cousin.
